How to recognise it: Hair dries without a repeating S-shape, ringlet, or coil through most of its length.
Common features to notice: It may lie close to the head or have more body depending on strand thickness and density; the A–C labels are informal ways people describe that variation.
General care practice, not a product rul: Use your scalp and ends as separate observations. Keep the routine light enough for your own roots, while conditioning the parts that feel dry or catch.

How to recognise it: Hair makes a visible loose or stronger S-pattern, often with a straighter-looking root area.
Common features to notice: The wave may appear more clearly in some sections than others and can change when brushed, slept on, or exposed to humidity.
General care practice, not a product rul: Try handling the hair gently after washing and notice whether dry brushing pulls apart the pattern you prefer. That is a general styling practice, not a requirement for every wave.

How to recognise it: Hair repeatedly forms loops, ringlets, or spring-like curves rather than only an open S.
Common features to notice: Different curl sizes can occur on one head, and the visible shape can change between wet and dry hair.
General care practice, not a product rul: Detangle with care when there is slip from water or conditioner if dry detangling makes your own hair snag. Keep the amount of handling guided by your result, not by a type label.

How to recognise it: Hair forms very tight coils, bends, or compact zig-zag-like turns; a stretched section can look much longer than its dry shape.
Common features to notice: Pattern, density, shrinkage, and tangling can vary sharply from one zone to another, so one small sample is not enough to describe the whole head.
General care practice, not a product rul: Work in manageable sections and observe where your hair catches or dries first. Reducing rough, dry manipulation is a general practice, not a rule that replaces your own routine.

How to recognise it: More than one pattern is consistently present: for example, a wavier crown with curlier lower sections, or looser front pieces with tighter areas elsewhere.
Common features to notice: Mixed pattern is common. It does not mean you have identified your hair incorrectly or need to force every area into one label.
General care practice, not a product rul: Record the areas separately and let their response guide your routine. A single product or one universal method is not guaranteed to suit every zone.
